edges.effect_quant: Early-life farm exposure is consistently associated with lower allergic disease burden. In Amish and Hutterite children, asthma and allergic sensitization were fourfold and sixfold less common in the Amish traditional-farm environment, and longitudinal farm cohorts show lower incident sensitization and lower allergy prevalence in exposed children.
edges.population: children growing up in traditional farm environments or with repeated early-life farm-related exposures
edges.mechanism: Traditional farm environments expose children to dense and diverse microbial signals, animal sheds, dust, and unprocessed farm products that appear to shape innate and adaptive immune maturation away from allergic sensitization. This is a classic human example of the farm effect and microbial immune training.
edges.summary: The evidence strongly supports a protective farm effect for allergic disease. Across U.S. and European cohorts, children with early-life farm exposure generally show less allergic sensitization, less asthma, and lower allergy prevalence than children in non-farm or industrialized-farm environments.
edges.caveats: Not every farming context is protective; industrialized large-animal operations and non-affluent settings can show different respiratory patterns. The clearest benefit appears in traditional farm environments with repeated early-life exposure rather than a single isolated farm-related factor.

evidence.citation: Stein MM et al 2016 N Engl J Med
evidence.notes: Innate Immunity and Asthma Risk in Amish and Hutterite Farm Children.

effect_quant.comparator: asthma prevalence in Amish versus Hutterite farm children; asthma was four times less common and allergic sensitization six times less common in the Amish environment

evidence.citation: Horak F et al 2002 Clin Exp Allergy
evidence.notes: Parental farming protects children against atopy: longitudinal evidence involving skin prick tests.

effect_quant.comparator: new occurrence of skin-prick-test positivity in children from farming versus non-farming families

evidence.citation: Waser M et al 2007 Clin Exp Allergy
evidence.notes: Inverse association of farm milk consumption with asthma and allergy in rural and suburban populations across Europe.

effect_quant.comparator: rhinoconjunctivitis in children who had ever consumed farm milk versus shop-purchased milk in the PARSIFAL study
